q7.answer: The API server generates the 32-byte random token, stores only its SHA-256 hash, builds the link https://<app>/reset?token=<raw token>, and puts the finished link in the email job it enqueues. The worker just sends that job, so the raw token exists only in the link/queue payload and never in the database.

q8.answer: The server computes sha256 of the token in the URL and selects the row by token_hash where used_at IS NULL and expires_at > now(). If a row is found the link is good and the password page is shown; if not (unknown, expired, used or superseded) the expired page is shown. The page-load check is read-only and burns nothing.

q9.answer: The count is derived from the password_reset_tokens table itself, with an index on (user_id, created_at): the API counts that user's rows with created_at in the last hour. Old requests drop out simply because they fall outside the rolling one-hour window; rows are not deleted within the hour (a nightly job can purge rows older than a day).

q10.answer: Inside the same transaction, after the rate-limit check passes and before inserting the new row, the API sets used_at=now() on all of that user's rows where used_at IS NULL, killing any earlier unused links. The new row is then inserted and committed with it, and the user row is locked with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE throughout.

q11.answer: In one transaction: the token is burned (used_at set), the user's password_hash is updated, and all of the user's sessions rows are deleted. The 'your password was changed' email is enqueued only after COMMIT, as step 4, so a failed enqueue cannot undo the reset.

q12.answer: The burn is a single conditional UPDATE ... WHERE token_hash=h AND used_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now() RETURNING user_id. Only one concurrent submission can match the row and get a user_id back; the other gets 0 rows, rolls back and sees the expired page.
